learningObjective: Trace one token through top-2 routing and distinguish the two experts that perform compute from all four expert parameter sets that remain resident in memory.
mediumRationale: A deterministic two-panel SVG is the smallest medium that can preserve token-to-expert paths, visibly distinguish selected from skipped experts, and juxtapose active compute with resident parameters. It keeps the routing rule and the memory-versus-FLOPs tradeoff in one static trace without requiring a runtime.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: a flowchart can show fan-out and combine, but it cannot compactly align router weights, selected-versus-skipped paths, and the resident-versus-active expert count at phone width.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: deterministic paths, direct weights, border styles, and a second accounting panel make both sparse execution and dense parameter residency spatially checkable.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: cards could compare counts, but connecting one token to its weighted expert paths and recombination would be less direct.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: changing token routes would add controls and state without improving the invariant lesson that only top-k experts compute while all N parameter sets remain stored.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: Mixtral and Switch Transformer contain architecture figures, but figure-reuse permission was not established and their layouts include more implementation detail than this learning objective needs.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: prose states k-of-N correctly, but readers must simultaneously imagine token-dependent routing and reconcile low active compute with high memory use.

pages.insight: The preceding recurrent-networks slide establishes the boundary before the transformer cluster and contains no conditional expert routing.
The transformer slide shows the standard dense encoder and decoder architecture, including one feed-forward sublayer through which every token passes.
The adjacent BERT slide discusses dense transformer representation learning and task heads but adds no sparse feed-forward mechanism.

The transformer-neural-nets slide explicitly identifies residual connections around the attention and feed-forward sublayers, providing the closest deck context for the FFN sublayer that MoE replaces.
The following GPT-X slide moves from architecture to instruction tuning and in-context learning, marking the end of the relevant local architecture discussion.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page Basic_ML_CS_concepts deck was searched page by page for mixture of experts, MoE, expert routing, top-k routing, conditional computation, sparse models, Switch Transformer, GShard, expert parallelism, all-to-all, and load balancing. No MoE-specific slide exists. Pages 100-104 were rendered and inspected directly because pages 101 and 103 are the nearest authoritative deck context: they show the dense transformer FFN sublayer that an MoE layer replaces. No deck screenshot, wording, coordinates, or embedded artwork was reused.

sources.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
sources.usage: Used as the foundational primary source for a sparsely gated layer that selects a small subset of experts per example and requires load-balancing mechanisms.
sources.license: No paper prose, equations, data, or figures were copied or adapted. Public arXiv access was not treated as permission to reuse source artwork.

sources.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
sources.usage: Used to cross-check token-wise routing, sparse expert activation, expert parallelism, capacity constraints, and the distinction between parameter count and per-token computation.
sources.license: No paper text, data, equation layout, or figure was copied or adapted. Figure-reuse rights were not assumed.

sources.title: Mixtral of Experts
sources.usage: Used to verify top-2 routing, softmax weights over selected experts, additive recombination, experts as transformer feed-forward blocks, and the total-versus-active parameter distinction.
sources.license: The model weights and accompanying source code are Apache 2.0, but that does not establish permission to reuse the paper's figures. No figure, prose, benchmark data, or layout was copied.

sourceReview.notes: The shipped schematic is independently authored and uses a generic four-expert teaching model rather than a paper architecture or empirical result. One token receives synthetic normalized top-2 weights 0.65 and 0.35 for E1 and E3; E2 and E4 have zero gate weight after top-k selection. All four expert parameter sets are shown as resident, while only E1 and E3 execute. The weighted symbolic output 0.65 E1(x) + 0.35 E3(x) is mathematically consistent and makes no claim about expert specialization.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, searched all 214 deck pages, inspected the nearest dense-transformer slide neighborhood, and checked three primary MoE papers. The hardest prose-only mental model is that sparse compute does not mean sparse storage, so the selected visual traces one top-2 route and then accounts for active versus resident experts.

implementation.accessibility: Each SVG panel has a linked title and full description. Expert numbers, selected and skipped labels, solid versus dashed paths, gate weights, and explicit 2-of-4 versus 4-of-4 counts carry all meaning without color. The established two-panel primitive stacks below 640 pixels; each 300-unit viewBox scales without a minimum width for readability at 390 CSS pixels. Existing theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print tokens force a light high-contrast palette.
